abstracts.abstract: Persistent memory technologies are fundamentally reshaping storage system design, yet existing reliability frameworks fail to capture the unique failure characteristics of byte-addressable non-volatile memories. This paper presents a novel reliability modeling paradigm that comprehensively captures the interaction between wear-out failures, power failure vulnerabilities, and data persistence guarantees in NVM-based storage systems. Our theoretical framework introduces a multi-layer stochastic model that jointly analyzes memory cell degradation, architectural vulnerability factors, and application-level persistence semantics. We formally derive closed-form expressions for the probability of data loss under various failure scenarios, enabling rigorous quantification of durability metrics previously considered intractable. The model reveals critical insights into the non-monotonic failure rate behavior exhibited by emerging storage-class memories, challenging conventional wisdom in archival storage reliability engineering. Extensive trace-driven simulations using production workloads demonstrate that our framework provides predictions within 8% of observed failure rates, while enabling system designers to explore reliability-performance tradeoffs analytically. This work establishes a foundational theoretical basis for designing next-generation storage systems that must guarantee data integrity across both normal operation and catastrophic failure events.

Erasure coding has become the dominant approach for achieving fault tolerance in large-scale distributed storage, but existing analytical models inadequately capture the performance implications of repair operations under realistic network conditions. This paper presents an enhanced analytical model that significantly improves upon prior work by incorporating heterogeneous bandwidth availability, correlated node failures, and partial repair parallelism into the reliability-performance tradeoff analysis. Our theoretical framework extends classical continuous-time Markov chain models with a novel state aggregation technique that maintains analytical tractability while capturing the complex dynamics of regenerating codes during reconstruction. We derive new expressions for mean time to data loss and expected repair latency that demonstrate up to 40% deviation from predictions made by existing models in production cloud storage environments. The analysis reveals optimal parity configurations that minimize storage overhead while satisfying specified durability targets under varying workload characteristics. We validate our model against empirical measurements from a 1000-node distributed storage cluster and demonstrate that the improved analytical framework enables more accurate capacity planning and reliability budgeting for enterprise storage deployments.

We present HydraStore, a fundamentally new storage architecture that reimagines data placement in hyperscale data centers by co-designing storage reliability with network topology awareness. Unlike traditional systems that treat storage nodes as independent failure domains, HydraStore exploits the structured nature of modern data center networks to create spatially-aware replication strategies that dramatically improve both durability and performance. The architecture introduces a topology-aware erasure coding scheme that places redundant data across network paths to minimize correlated failure exposure while maintaining low-latency access. We implement HydraStore as a middleware layer that transparently augments existing distributed storage systems, requiring no modifications to application code. Our prototype deployment across a 500-server cluster demonstrates a 3.2x improvement in storage efficiency compared to conventional replication while maintaining sub-millisecond tail latencies for read operations. Under simulated datacenter-scale failures, HydraStore achieves 99.9999% availability, surpassing the durability targets of production archival storage systems. This architecture represents a paradigm shift from node-centric to network-centric reliability design, opening new research directions in storage system optimization.

Data deduplication has emerged as an essential technique for reducing storage costs in backup and archival workloads, yet existing systems suffer from fragmented access patterns and metadata bottlenecks that severely degrade restore performance. This paper presents FragmentDB, a deduplication-aware storage system that substantially improves both storage efficiency and retrieval performance through intelligent container management and learned data placement. FragmentDB introduces a novel similarity-aware containerization strategy that groups related data chunks based on temporal and content similarity, dramatically reducing fragmentation during restores. We design a lightweight machine learning model that predicts access patterns from workload characteristics, enabling proactive prefetching of deduplicated data segments. The system incorporates a hybrid indexing architecture that separates hot and cold metadata to eliminate scalability bottlenecks inherent in traditional data deduplication approaches. Experiments using production backup traces from enterprise storage systems show that FragmentDB achieves 35% higher deduplication ratios than state-of-the-art systems while reducing average restore time by 60%. The design demonstrates that significant improvements in both storage efficiency and performance are achievable through co-optimization of deduplication and storage management, benefiting applications from archival storage to cloud backup services.
